Imperial
ĭm-pē´rĭ-al
adj. (pertaining to an empire or an emperor; sovereign in the highest civil degree)
Latin imperium, command, dominion. The New Testament was written inside one empire, addressed to subjects of it, and its Lord was executed by its officer.

Biblical Definition

The imperial power frames the whole New Testament. It sets the scene of the nativity: “there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed” (Luk 2:1). It is invoked against Christ: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). It is used by Paul: “I appeal unto Caesar” (Act 25:11). It is penetrated by the gospel: “All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household” (Php 4:22). And it is judged: to the beast “power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations” (Rev 13:7) — given, which is the last word on every empire.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines imperial as pertaining to an empire or to an emperor; royal; and belonging to a supreme or sovereign power, as imperial authority.

expand to see more

IMPERIAL, a. Pertaining to an empire, or to an emperor; as an imperial dominion; imperial city.

2. Royal; belonging to a monarch; as an imperial crown.

3. Pertaining to supreme authority; sovereign; supreme; as imperial power; imperial authority.

IMPERIOUS, a. Commanding; dictatorial; haughty; arrogant; overbearing.

Key Scripture

Luk 2:1 — "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed."

John 19:15 — "But they cried out, Away with him, away with him, crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucify your King? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Caesar."

Act 25:11 — "For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar."

Php 4:22 — "All the saints salute you, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household."

Rev 13:7 — "And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations."

Modern Corruption

Political power is treated as ultimate by those who hold it and by those who fear it, and Revelation says it was given.

expand to see more

Luke 2:1 is a study in what the Bible thinks of imperial power. Caesar Augustus, the most powerful man alive, issues a decree that all the world should be taxed — and the effect recorded in Scripture is that it moved a pregnant carpenter's wife eighty miles to the town a prophet had named seven centuries earlier. The emperor is a real cause and he is also an instrument, and he does not know it. That is the perspective Christians are given on political power: entirely real, entirely serious, and not the level at which the decisive things are happening.

John 19:15 is the darkest sentence in the Gospel and it is spoken by the chief priests: We have no king but Caesar. To secure a crucifixion, the custodians of Israel's hope renounced the hope. That is what a captive religious establishment sounds like, and every church that has traded its confession for the protection or approval of a government has said some version of it. The line is worth keeping in mind whenever the church finds itself needing the state's goodwill.

Philippians 4:22 is the counter-image and it is almost a joke. Paul, a prisoner of the empire, closes a letter with greetings from the saints, chiefly they that are of Caesar's household — the slaves and officials of the imperial palace, converted. The gospel got in. Within three centuries the empire that executed its Founder was arguing about His nature at a council, which introduced a different set of problems, but the point stands: Revelation 13:7 says power was given to the beast, and what is given can be withdrawn, and no empire has ever outlasted the church it persecuted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Kaisar (G2541), Caesar; dogma (G1378), a decree; epikaleomai (G1941), to appeal; edothe auto (G1325), it was given unto him.

expand to see more

Greek dogma (G1378) — a decree; Luke 2:1, Acts 16:4, 17:7, Colossians 2:14.

Greek Kaisara epikaloumai (G1941) — I appeal unto Caesar; Acts 25:11, 25:21, 26:32, 28:19.

Greek edothe auto (G1325) — there was given unto him; Revelation 13:5, 13:7, 13:14–15.

Usage

"“A decree from Caesar Augustus” — and it moved a woman to Bethlehem."

"“We have no king but Caesar” — said by the chief priests."

"“They that are of Caesar's household” — from a prisoner of the empire."
